assessment.name: Year 8 English Autumn assessment
assessment.sections: Monday 30 November, period 3, 50 minutes, on paper. Expect reading questions and a piece of writing.
assessment.weighting: Autumn 1: Romeo and Juliet. Autumn 2: Opinion writing on the climate crisis. Check with the teacher which part carries most marks.

mock.note: 25 questions on Romeo and Juliet and persuasive writing. Practise a full piece of writing in the Written practice tab.

leitner_plan.new: Romeo and Juliet plot and characters (5)
Romeo and Juliet themes, quotes, analysis (5)

leitner_plan.quiz: English mock, then plan one piece of writing

cards.title: Plot in five acts
cards.question: What happens in each act of Romeo and Juliet?
points: Act 1: Montagues and Capulets fight in Verona. Romeo, sad about Rosaline, meets Juliet at the Capulet party.
Act 2: The balcony scene. Friar Laurence secretly marries them.
Act 3: Tybalt kills Mercutio; Romeo kills Tybalt and is banished. Juliet's father arranges her marriage to Paris.
Act 4: Friar Laurence gives Juliet a potion to fake her death.
Act 5: Romeo does not get the Friar's message, finds Juliet 'dead' and poisons himself. Juliet wakes and stabs herself. The families make peace.
cards.watch_out: Act 3 Scene 1 is the turning point, the play changes from comedy to tragedy.
cards.hook: Meet, Marry, Murder, Medicine, Mortality: the five acts.
cards.grade9: Refer to structure, for example the prologue tells us the ending, so the audience watches with dramatic irony.

cards.title: Main characters
cards.question: Who are the main characters and what are they like?
points: Romeo: passionate, impulsive, falls in love quickly. Juliet: nearly 14, grows from obedient to bold and decisive.
Mercutio: Romeo's witty friend, curses both houses as he dies. Tybalt: Juliet's hot-headed, violent cousin.
Friar Laurence: well-meaning priest whose plans go wrong. The Nurse: Juliet's comic, loving servant who later lets her down.
Lord Capulet: controlling father who becomes furious when Juliet refuses Paris.
cards.watch_out: Write about characters as constructs, for example Shakespeare presents Tybalt as..., not Tybalt is a real person.
cards.hook: Mercutio is Mercurial (quick and changeable). Tybalt is Trouble.
cards.grade9: Track change, how Juliet's language becomes more confident and independent as the play goes on.

cards.title: Theme of fate
cards.question: How does Shakespeare present fate in Romeo and Juliet?
points: The prologue calls the lovers star-crossed, so their deaths seem fated from the start.
Romeo has a feeling before the party that something terrible will begin there.
After killing Tybalt, Romeo cries that he is fortune's fool, blaming fate.
Chance events, like the Friar's undelivered letter, push the tragedy on.
cards.watch_out: Balance fate against choices. Characters also make rash decisions.
cards.hook: Star-crossed = stars against them. Elizabethans believed stars shaped lives.
cards.grade9: Link to the big question, how much can you control your own fate? Argue both ways, then decide.

cards.title: Love and hate
cards.question: How are love and hate shown, and how are they linked?
points: The play opens with hate (the feud) and ends with love (the families reconcile).
Juliet says her only love has sprung from her only hate, showing the two are tangled together.
Romeo's love for Rosaline is shallow and full of clichés; his love for Juliet is deeper and shown in a shared sonnet.
Violence and love both happen quickly and passionately.
cards.watch_out: Oxymorons (opposites together) show this conflict, such as loving hate.
cards.hook: Oxymoron = sharp-dull in Greek: opposites side by side.
cards.grade9: Analyse the shared sonnet at their first meeting, the form itself shows they are perfectly matched.

cards.title: Conflict, youth and age, and context
cards.question: What other themes and context should you write about?
points: Conflict: public fights in the streets of Verona; private conflict between Juliet and her father.
Youth and age: the young act on impulse; the old give advice or control (the Friar says wisely and slow).
Context: Elizabethan England was patriarchal; daughters were expected to obey their fathers and marry the man their father chose.
Honour mattered to men, which is why Romeo must avenge Mercutio.
cards.watch_out: Only use context that helps explain the text. Do not bolt on history facts.
cards.grade9: Use context to explain why Lord Capulet's anger would shock or not shock an Elizabethan audience.

cards.title: Key quotations to learn
cards.question: Can you complete and explain these short quotations?
points: A pair of star-crossed lovers (Prologue): fate.
My only love sprung from my only hate (Juliet, Act 1): love and hate.
A plague o' both your houses (Mercutio, Act 3): blame and conflict.
O, I am fortune's fool (Romeo, Act 3): fate.
Wisely and slow; they stumble that run fast (Friar Laurence, Act 2): youth and age.
cards.watch_out: Short quotations are easier to remember and analyse than long ones.
cards.hook: Pick one word from each quotation to zoom in on: star-crossed, hate, plague, fool, stumble.
cards.grade9: Zoom in on single words and explore more than one meaning.

cards.title: Writing an analytical paragraph
cards.question: How do you write a strong paragraph about Romeo and Juliet?
points: What: make a point that answers the question.
How: embed a short quotation and name a method (metaphor, oxymoron, imagery, dramatic irony).
Why: explain the effect on the audience and Shakespeare's purpose.
Zoom in on one word, then link to context or the big question.

example.heading: Model sentence starters
lines: This makes the audience feel ... because ...

cards.watch_out: Do not just retell the story. Every paragraph must analyse.
cards.grade9: Offer an alternative reading, alternatively, this could suggest...

cards.title: Dramatic methods
cards.question: Which dramatic and language methods does Shakespeare use?
points: Dramatic irony: the audience knows something the characters do not (the prologue reveals the ending).
Soliloquy: a character speaks thoughts aloud alone on stage.
Sonnet: a 14-line love poem form; Romeo and Juliet's first words to each other make a sonnet.
Imagery of light and dark: Romeo compares Juliet to the sun and to a bright jewel.
cards.watch_out: Name the method, then explain its effect. Naming alone earns little.
cards.grade9: Explain why Shakespeare chose that method at that moment in the play.

cards.title: Answering the big question
cards.question: How do you plan an answer to how far can you control your own fate?
points: Decide your argument first (thesis).
Paragraph 1: evidence that fate controls them (prologue, fortune's fool).
Paragraph 2: evidence that choices cause the tragedy (rash marriage, killing Tybalt).
Paragraph 3: your judgement, for example fate sets the stage but characters' haste completes the tragedy.
cards.watch_out: A balanced answer still needs a clear conclusion.
cards.grade9: Use conceptual language, Shakespeare suggests that..., implying that...

cards.title: Key vocabulary for the play
cards.question: What do these words mean, and how can you use them about the play?
points: Feud: a long, bitter quarrel between families.
Banished: sent away and forbidden to return.
Impulsive: acting without thinking.
Tragedy: a play where the hero's downfall ends in death.
Patriarchal: a society controlled by men.
cards.watch_out: Use these words in your answers, not just in your notes.
cards.grade9: Use precise words like impetuous or capricious for higher marks.

cards.title: Purpose, audience, form
cards.question: What should you decide before writing an opinion piece?
points: Purpose: to argue or persuade.
Audience: who is reading (students, headteacher, MP, newspaper readers). Change formality to suit them.
Form: article, speech, letter or blog. Each has layout features.
Letter: address, Dear..., Yours sincerely. Speech: address the audience directly. Article: headline and subheading.
cards.watch_out: Underline purpose, audience and form in the task before you plan.
cards.grade9: Keep the tone consistent and suited to the audience throughout.

cards.title: Persuasive devices
cards.question: Which persuasive techniques can you use?
points: Direct address (you), Alliteration, Facts, Opinions, Rhetorical questions, Emotive language, Statistics, Triplets (rule of three).
Also: anecdote (a short personal story), counterargument, imperatives (act now).
Use devices for a purpose, not just to tick them off.

example.heading: Example
lines: Can we really stand by while our planet burns? (rhetorical question, emotive)

cards.watch_out: Do not invent silly statistics. Use believable, careful ones such as most scientists agree.
cards.hook: DAFOREST: Direct address, Alliteration, Facts, Opinions, Rhetorical questions, Emotive language, Statistics, Triplets.
cards.grade9: Combine devices in one powerful sentence and vary sentence length for impact.

cards.title: Structure of an opinion piece
cards.question: How do you structure an opinion article or speech?
points: Introduction: a hook and your clear opinion.
Paragraphs 2 to 3: your strongest arguments with evidence and examples.
Paragraph 4: counterargument, then rebut it (some people say..., however...).
Conclusion: a call to action and a memorable final line, often linking back to the opening.
cards.watch_out: One main idea per paragraph, with a clear topic sentence.
cards.hook: Hook, Argue, Argue, Answer back, Act (HAAAA).
cards.grade9: Use a cyclical structure, return to the image or question from the opening in your final line.

cards.title: Arguments about the climate crisis
cards.question: What arguments can you use about the climate crisis?
points: Burning fossil fuels increases carbon dioxide, which traps heat and warms the planet.
Effects include extreme weather, rising sea levels, and harm to wildlife and people.
Young people can make a difference: Greta Thunberg began a school strike alone and inspired millions (reading canon: No One is Too Small to Make a Difference).
Actions: renewable energy, less waste, walking or cycling, eating less meat, pressure on governments.
cards.watch_out: Keep science accurate. Use facts you know are true, such as rising global temperatures.
cards.grade9: Balance individual actions with the need for government and business action.

cards.title: Counterargument and rebuttal
cards.question: How do you deal with the other side of the argument?
points: Show you understand the other view, which makes you sound fair and reasonable.
Some might argue that one person's actions are too small to matter.
However, this ignores the fact that... (rebut with evidence or an example).
Finish the paragraph by returning to your own view.
cards.watch_out: Keep the counterargument short and the rebuttal longer.
cards.grade9: Use concessive phrases, admittedly, while it is true that, nevertheless.

cards.title: Ambitious sentences and punctuation
cards.question: How can you vary sentences and punctuation to impress?
points: Short sentences for impact: Time is running out.
Colons to introduce: There is one solution: act now.
Semicolons to link related ideas: The ice is melting; the seas are rising.
Start sentences in different ways: with a verb ending in -ing, an adverb, a question.
cards.watch_out: Every sentence still needs correct capital letters and full stops.
cards.grade9: Use a short one-line paragraph after a long one for dramatic effect.

cards.title: Discourse markers
cards.question: Which linking words make an argument flow?
points: Adding: furthermore, moreover, in addition.
Contrasting: however, on the other hand, nevertheless.
Cause and effect: therefore, consequently, as a result.
Concluding: ultimately, in conclusion, above all.
cards.watch_out: Do not start every paragraph with firstly, secondly, thirdly.
cards.hook: FATCAT: Furthermore, Additionally, Therefore, Consequently, As a result, Thus.
cards.grade9: Choose the marker that shows the exact logical link between ideas.

cards.title: Checking and planning in the exam
cards.question: How do you use your time in the writing task?
points: 5 minutes: plan (PAF, opinion, 4 to 5 paragraph ideas).
30 minutes: write.
5 minutes: check spelling, punctuation and paragraphing.
cards.watch_out: An unfinished piece loses marks. Plan so you reach a conclusion.
cards.grade9: Plan your final line first so your ending is strong.

written.q: Write an article for your school newspaper arguing that young people can make a difference to the climate crisis.
model: Clear opinion stated in the opening with a hook (4)
Two or three well-developed arguments with evidence and examples (4)
Range of persuasive devices used for effect (4)
Varied sentences, accurate punctuation, paragraphs, and a strong call to action (4)

written.q: How does Shakespeare present fate in Romeo and Juliet? Refer to at least two moments in the play.
model: Clear argument about fate and choice (3)
Relevant short quotations, such as star-crossed and fortune's fool (3)
Analysis of words and methods, such as prologue and dramatic irony (3)
Context, such as Elizabethan belief in the stars, used to explain meaning (3)

written.q: How does Shakespeare present Lord Capulet's relationship with Juliet?
model: Point on how he controls her marriage (2)
Short quotation or reference to his anger in Act 3 (2)

written.q: Write the opening two paragraphs of a speech to your year group persuading them to cut waste at school.

exam_tips.timing: 50 minutes. Read the questions first. Spend time in proportion to the marks.
section_a: For reading questions, use short quotations and say what one key word suggests.
Write about Shakespeare's choices, not just what happens.
What, How, Why in every paragraph.
section_b: Plan for 5 minutes using PAF and a paragraph list.
Use at least four DAFOREST devices, with purpose.
Leave 5 minutes to check capital letters, full stops, commas and paragraphing.
grade9: Ask yourself: can I explain why, not just what?
Say what Shakespeare chose, then why it matters. A contrast between two characters shows their different values.
In opinion writing give a claim, a reason and an example in every paragraph.

mcq.q: Where is Romeo and Juliet set?
mcq.e: The play is set in Verona, Italy.

mcq.q: Whom does Romeo love at the start of the play?
mcq.e: He meets Juliet at the party.

mcq.q: Who marries Romeo and Juliet?
Who kills Mercutio?
What is Romeo's punishment for killing Tybalt?
mcq.e: He is sent away from Verona.

mcq.q: Whom does Lord Capulet want Juliet to marry?
What does Friar Laurence give Juliet?
mcq.a: A potion to make her seem dead

mcq.q: Why doesn't Romeo get the Friar's message?
mcq.a: The messenger is held up by the plague

mcq.q: What does star-crossed mean?
What is dramatic irony?
mcq.a: When the audience knows something the characters do not
mcq.e: The prologue tells us the ending.

mcq.q: Which scene is the turning point of the play?
mcq.a: Act 3 Scene 1, the deaths of Mercutio and Tybalt

mcq.q: Who says A plague o' both your houses?
mcq.e: He blames both families as he dies.

mcq.q: What is an oxymoron?
What does patriarchal mean?
Which method is a 14-line love poem?
mcq.e: Romeo and Juliet share a sonnet when they meet.

mcq.q: Which character is described as hot-headed and violent?
What is the purpose of an opinion piece?
mcq.e: It tries to change the reader's mind.

mcq.q: Which is a rhetorical question?
mcq.a: Can we really ignore our burning planet?
mcq.e: It is asked for effect, not an answer.

mcq.q: Which is an example of a triplet?
mcq.a: Cleaner air, cooler cities and healthier lives
mcq.e: A list of three for emphasis.

mcq.q: What does counterargument mean?
mcq.a: An opposing view you then answer

mcq.q: Which is a discourse marker for contrast?
Which marker shows a result?
Which ending is a call to action?
mcq.a: Turn off the lights, walk to school and speak up today.
mcq.e: It tells the reader what to do.

mcq.q: What does PAF stand for?
Which is the correct sign-off for a formal letter that starts Dear Sir?
mcq.e: Yours sincerely is used with a name.

mcq.q: Which punctuation introduces an explanation or list?
mcq.e: There is one solution: act now.

mcq.q: What is emotive language?
mcq.a: Words chosen to make the reader feel strongly

mcq.q: Greta Thunberg is known for
mcq.a: Starting a school strike for the climate
mcq.e: Her speeches are in the reading canon book.

mcq.q: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
mcq.a: The ice is melting; the seas are rising.
w: The ice is; melting the seas
mcq.e: A semicolon joins two related full sentences.

vocab.example: Romeo's impulsive marriage leads to disaster.
The feud between the families causes the tragedy.

vocab.meaning: Forced to leave and not allowed back
Certain to happen and unable to be avoided
vocab.example: The prologue makes their deaths seem inevitable.
Climate change is an urgent problem.

vocab.meaning: Able to continue without damaging the planet
vocab.example: We need sustainable ways to travel.

vocab.meaning: To make someone agree or act
vocab.example: Use evidence to persuade your reader.
Rising seas are one consequence of warming.
Juliet becomes defiant when she refuses Paris.
